canonical_question: Why was Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) selected over mechanical cutting for the high-temperature tensile specimens, and does it affect the gauge length surface integrity?

question_variants.question: Why was Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) selected over mechanical cutting for the high-temperature tensile specimens, and does it affect the gauge length surface integrity?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text confirms that Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) was employed to obtain flat specimens for high temperature tensile tests, but it does not explain why EDM was selected over mechanical cutting, nor does it address the effect on gauge length surface integrity.

answers.answer: Electrical discharge machining was employed to obtain flat specimens for high temperature tensile tests. The provided text does not contain a rationale for selecting EDM over mechanical cutting or data on its effect on the gauge length surface integrity.
answers.material: Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6
answers.boundary_limitation: No comparison with mechanical cutting or surface integrity analysis provided
evidence_spans: The alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 exhibited a dendritic microstructure after the casting process.
Subsequent annealing for 50 h at 900 °C lead to a three-phase microstructure
Figure 1 a) shows the large (several 10 µm), randomly distributed Heusler type phase, with its characteristic needle-like shape and a volume-fraction of <5%.
